lessons.title: Frame Anatomy: Top Bar, Bottom Bar, Side Bars
lessons.body: A bee frame is a rectangular wooden structure that holds honeycomb. It has four parts: top bar, bottom bar, and two side bars. The top bar is the longest piece, usually 48.3 cm (19 inches) for a standard Langstroth hive. It has a thicker profile to support the weight of honey and to hang on the hive body's frame rest. The bottom bar is the same length but thinner, often 1.9 cm (3/4 inch) wide and 1 cm (3/8 inch) thick. The side bars are 23.2 cm (9 1/8 inches) tall, connecting the top and bottom bars. They have a notch at the top to fit under the top bar and a hole or slot at the bottom for the bottom bar. In Africa, many beekeepers use local timber like cypress, pine, or eucalyptus. Avoid termite-prone woods like soft mango. Cut all pieces accurately; a frame that is 2 mm off will not sit properly in the hive. Use a tape measure, pencil, and a mitre saw or hand saw. Sand rough edges to prevent bee injuries. The top bar often has a groove on the underside to hold foundation. The side bars may have holes for wiring. Understanding these parts helps you build strong, interchangeable frames. A well-built frame lasts many years and makes hive inspections easy.

lessons.title: Cutting and Assembling Wooden Frames
lessons.body: To cut frames, start with dry, straight timber. Use a table saw or circular saw for speed, but a hand saw works fine. Set a stop block to cut multiple pieces to the same length. For a standard Langstroth frame, cut top bars to 48.3 cm, bottom bars to 48.3 cm, and side bars to 23.2 cm. You need two side bars per frame. Cut a notch at the top of each side bar to fit the top bar. The notch is usually 1.5 cm deep and 2 cm wide. At the bottom, cut a slot for the bottom bar. Sand all pieces with 80-grit sandpaper. Assembly: apply waterproof wood glue (like Titebond III) to all joints. Use a frame jig to hold pieces square. Nail with 4 cm (1.5 inch) galvanised nails: two nails through each side bar into the top bar, and two into the bottom bar. Pre-drill holes to avoid splitting. Check for square by measuring diagonals; they must be equal. Let glue dry for 24 hours. In Africa, use nails that won't rust in humid conditions. If using local hardwood, pre-drill all holes. A good frame is rigid and does not twist. Build at least 10 frames per hive box. Stack them flat to dry. Poor assembly leads to burr comb and broken frames.

lessons.title: Wiring Frames for Strength
lessons.body: Wiring a frame reinforces the comb so it doesn't break during extraction or hot weather. You need frame wire (26 or 28 gauge, stainless steel or galvanised), a wire embedder (spur or electric), and wire cutters. First, drill four small holes in the side bars: two near the top and two near the bottom. They should be about 1 cm from the edges. Thread one end of the wire through a hole and secure it with a small nail or a figure-eight knot. Pull the wire across to the opposite hole, then back, creating a zigzag pattern: two horizontal wires across the frame. Keep the wire tight; it should twang when plucked. Use a wire tensioner or a nail to twist the wire at the end. For embedding, place a sheet of wax foundation on the frame. Run a spur embedder (a tool with a small wheel) along the wires, pressing them into the wax. Alternatively, use an electric embedder that heats the wire. In Africa, many beekeepers use a 12V car battery and a length of resistance wire to heat and embed. Do not overheat; wax melts at 63Â°C. Let the wax cool and set. Check that wires are embedded but not cutting through. Properly wired frames last many seasons and produce straight comb.

lessons.title: Installing Wax Foundation: Crimp-Wire and Pin
lessons.body: Wax foundation is a thin sheet of beeswax with a hexagon pattern. It guides bees to build straight comb. You can install it using crimp-wire or pins. Crimp-wire method: after wiring the frame, place the foundation on the wires. Use a crimping tool (or a small pliers) to press the wire into the wax. Start at one end and work along each wire. The wire should sit just below the surface. Then, use a spur embedder to press the wire deeper. For extra security, use a hot wire embedder. Pin method: use foundation pins (small metal pins with a flat head) or a stapler. Place the foundation on the frame and push pins through the wax into the top bar and side bars. Space pins every 5 cm. In Africa, many beekeepers make their own foundation using a silicone mould and melted beeswax. When installing, do it in a warm room (25-30Â°C) so the wax is pliable. Do not install in direct sun; it will melt. If foundation is brittle, warm it slightly. Ensure the foundation is centred and flat. Bees will draw comb from it. A well-installed foundation saves the colony energy and reduces drone comb. Replace foundation every 2-3 years to avoid disease buildup.

lessons.title: Building Foundationless Frames with Starter Strips
lessons.body: Foundationless frames have no full wax sheet, only a starter strip at the top. This allows bees to build natural comb, which many African beekeepers prefer because it saves money and wax. To make a starter strip, cut a piece of beeswax foundation 2-3 cm tall and as wide as the top bar. Alternatively, use a wooden strip or a plastic strip. Attach it to the underside of the top bar using melted beeswax or small nails. You can also run a bead of melted wax along the top bar and press the strip into it. The strip acts as a guide. For strength, wire the frame as usual, but leave the wires exposed. Bees will build comb around the wires. Another method is to cut a V-shaped groove in the top bar and pour melted wax into it. The bees will follow the wax line. In Africa, use local beeswax from your own hives. Make sure the starter strip is straight and centred. When placing the frame in the hive, ensure it is level. Bees build comb downward. Check frames every week; if comb is crooked, straighten it early. Foundationless frames require more frequent inspections but produce high-quality wax. They are ideal for top-bar hives and for beekeepers who want to avoid buying foundation.

lessons.title: Assembling Plastic Frames and Foundations
lessons.body: Plastic frames and foundations are one-piece units, often made of food-grade plastic. They are durable, resistant to wax moths, and easy to clean. To assemble, you simply snap the plastic foundation into the plastic frame. No wiring or embedding is needed. Some plastic frames come pre-assembled; others require you to fit the foundation into the frame's grooves. Use your thumbs to press the foundation into the frame until it clicks. Make sure it is seated evenly. Plastic frames are heavier than wood but last many years. They are ideal for African beekeepers who lack woodworking tools or who want to reduce labour. However, bees may be slow to accept plastic, especially if it is smooth. To encourage acceptance, coat the foundation with a thin layer of melted beeswax. Use a paintbrush or dip the foundation in warm wax. Let it dry before placing in the hive. Plastic frames can be cleaned with a hive tool and warm water. Do not use boiling water; it will warp. In hot African climates, plastic can become brittle; store them out of direct sun. They are also less forgiving if dropped. Use plastic frames in all hive boxes for uniformity. They are a good choice for beginners and for areas with high humidity.

quiz.q: What is the standard length of a top bar for a Langstroth frame?
quiz.explanation: The top bar of a standard Langstroth frame is 48.3 cm (19 inches) long.

quiz.q: Which part of the frame has a notch to fit under the top bar?
quiz.explanation: Side bars have a notch at the top to fit under the top bar.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid using termite-prone wood for frames?
options: C) It weakens and breaks easily
D) It is hard to cut
quiz.explanation: Termite-prone wood weakens and breaks, compromising the frame's strength.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a frame jig during assembly?
quiz.explanation: A frame jig holds the frame pieces square while nailing and gluing.

quiz.q: How many nails are typically used per side bar joint?
quiz.explanation: Two nails are used: one into the top bar and one into the bottom bar.

quiz.q: What type of glue is recommended for frame assembly?
quiz.explanation: Waterproof wood glue (like Titebond III) withstands humidity in the hive.

quiz.q: How can you check if a frame is square?
quiz.explanation: Measuring the diagonals; if equal, the frame is square.

quiz.q: What gauge wire is commonly used for frame wiring?
quiz.explanation: 26 or 28 gauge wire is standard for beehive frames.

quiz.q: How many horizontal wires are typically run across a frame?
quiz.explanation: Two horizontal wires are standard for strength.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a spur embedder?
options: B) To press wire into wax
quiz.explanation: A spur embedder presses the wire into the wax foundation.

quiz.q: At what temperature does beeswax melt?
quiz.explanation: Beeswax melts at about 63Â°C.

quiz.q: What is a common alternative power source for electric embedding in Africa?
quiz.explanation: A 12V car battery with resistance wire is commonly used.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of wax foundation?
options: B) It guides bees to build straight comb
quiz.explanation: Wax foundation guides bees to build straight, uniform comb.

quiz.q: Which tool is used for the crimp-wire method?
quiz.explanation: A crimping tool presses the wire into the wax.

quiz.q: How often should foundation be replaced?
quiz.explanation: Replace foundation every 2-3 years to avoid disease buildup.

quiz.q: What is a starter strip in foundationless frames?
options: A) A full sheet of wax
B) A small piece of wax at the top
quiz.explanation: A starter strip is a small piece of wax or wood at the top to guide comb.

quiz.q: Why might African beekeepers prefer foundationless frames?
options: A) They save money on wax
C) They are easier to inspect
quiz.explanation: Foundationless frames save money because they require less wax.

quiz.q: How can you attach a starter strip to the top bar?
quiz.explanation: Melted beeswax, nails, or glue can all be used.

quiz.q: What is a disadvantage of foundationless frames?
options: A) They require more frequent inspections
quiz.explanation: Foundationless frames need more frequent inspections to correct crooked comb.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of plastic frames?
options: B) They are durable and easy to clean
quiz.explanation: Plastic frames are durable, resistant to wax moths, and easy to clean.

quiz.q: How do you assemble a plastic frame?
quiz.explanation: Plastic foundations snap into the plastic frame.

quiz.q: Why should you coat plastic foundation with wax?
options: B) To encourage bees to accept it
quiz.explanation: A thin wax coating encourages bees to accept plastic foundation.

quiz.q: How should you clean plastic frames?
options: B) Warm water and hive tool
quiz.explanation: Warm water and a hive tool are safe for cleaning plastic frames.

quiz.q: What happens to plastic frames in hot African climates?
quiz.explanation: Plastic can become brittle in hot, dry conditions.

quiz.q: What is the standard height of a Langstroth side bar?
quiz.explanation: Side bars are 23.2 cm (9 1/8 inches) tall.

quiz.q: Which wood is recommended for African beehive frames?
quiz.explanation: Cypress, pine, and eucalyptus are recommended; mango is termite-prone.

quiz.q: Why pre-drill holes before nailing?
quiz.explanation: Pre-drilling prevents the wood from splitting, especially hardwoods.

quiz.q: How long should glued frames dry before use?
quiz.explanation: Let glue dry for 24 hours for maximum strength.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of wiring a frame?
quiz.explanation: Wiring reinforces the comb so it doesn't break during extraction.

quiz.q: What is a common mistake when installing wax foundation?
quiz.explanation: Installing in direct sun can melt the foundation.
